props.title: Mrs. Dalloway
props.initialSlug: One woman's inner journey through a single London day

sections.content: Marleen Gorris's adaptation of Virginia Woolf's modernist masterpiece showcases Vanessa Redgrave's commanding performance as Clarissa Dalloway, capturing the novel's stream-of-consciousness style through deft parallel editing and flashbacks. Like Michael Cunningham's later adaptation The Hours (2002), the film wrestles with women's inner lives and societal constraints. Where Orlando (1992) took Woolf's gender-bending fantasy into surreal territory, Mrs. Dalloway grounds itself in the subtle psychological realism of post-WWI London, examining how the trauma of war ripples through society.

sections.content: The film's parallel structure between Clarissa Dalloway and shell-shocked veteran Septimus Warren Smith creates a devastating commentary on British society's treatment of mental illness and trauma. This technique influenced later literary adaptations like Atonement (2007) and The English Patient (1996), which similarly weave between timeframes to explore memory and regret. Eileen Atkins's screenplay maintains Woolf's subtle critique of class and gender roles while making the narrative accessible to modern audiences. SUBHEAD: Literary Modernism on Screen

Mrs. Dalloway belongs to a vital tradition of films adapting modernist literature, including The Dead (1987), John Huston's take on James Joyce, and Between the Acts (2002). These films face the challenge of translating experimental prose into visual language. Gorris employs subtle camera movements and careful sound design to suggest interior monologue without resorting to voiceover, creating a more immersive experience than many literary adaptations.
